utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Anna Richterova and Kapila Waidyaratne for the Prosecution assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Milan Trbojevic with my associate Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you too. Are there any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: There is one matter which I would like to raise, Your Honour. There was -- with regard to the next witness, Mr. Muharem Murselovic who testified in the Stakic trial we intend to submit his previous testimony from the Stakic trial and with the Defence counsel we agreed to certain facts and there was an area which there was -- which was in dispute and which we have submitted to the ruling from the Chamber. We would expect a decision from the Chamber. Therefore, after that, we could see as to whether we could redact or whether we should leave it in the transcript before we submit the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What are you referring to? The only information that I have is that there seems to be just one very short sentence in the transcript on page 2875, which the Defence object to or would like to see redacted from the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: From 2875, line 4 to 2876, line 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: From page 2875, line 4, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: To 2876, line 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 2876, line?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Ten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You would like these to be redacted, correct, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a text which Mr. Ackerman wrote requesting it, but it is at odds with what you just read out to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I mean, if you want a decision from us you need to be categoric and clear. Are we talking of the same two pages or not? Because we can't hand down a decision if you're not agreeing on the text that you would like to see redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I would point out the relevant lines to Your Honour from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have it marked from page 2875, where Judge Schomburg starts with: "Once again a question far away from judicial questions," and the rest of the page follows and you go to the next page, until line 10, because the rest of that page and part of the page that follows has already been redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I'm referring to the pages that Your Honour has just referred to. The lines. 2875, from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, actually, the document that I have also shows a marking right through until page 2878, at the bottom. And I think it is natural that it includes also the last part of page 2878 because, as you see, "what I considered him to be amongst the most responsible" so I think it's a logical sequence of --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: We have agreed as Your Honour pointed out in 2876 from page 11 -- line 11, to 2878, up to 25, if I may say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Trbojevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Line 19, I'm sorry, Your Honour, line 19, which we have agreed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will agree with my learned friend. I will accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Accept what? The indication of the pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I agree with what the Prosecutor has just proposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, our decision is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the decision of the Chamber is to redact in its entirety the contents of the transcript starting from page 2875, line 4, up to and including page 2878, line 25. No, no, 25. I'm redacting this as well. Because it's got nothing to do with -- it's to do with Dr. Stakic. So and if you are -- of course you are free to put any questions, but that's easy and we could have avoided all this. Let's bring in the witness. The witness has no protective measures, if I am right, Madam Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, there are no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Murselovic. And welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence and before you do so, you are kindly requested to read out the text of the solemn declaration that is going to be handed to you by the usher. That is equivalent to an oath and is your undertaking in front of this Tribunal that in the course of your testimony you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: May I have your permission to proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. I understand that the witness knows you already.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I don't need to introduce you to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I thank you. Examined by Mr. Waidyaratne:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, good morning to you. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified in another trial, in the trial against Milomir Stakic, on the 6th, 8th and the 9th of May, in this year, the year 2002?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you reviewed your testimony from -- in that -- from that trial by listening to the audiotapes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stand by that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, I will today ask you some questions to clarify certain things and also ask questions with regard to some additional information, but before that, to introduce you to the Chamber, I will ask a preliminary couple of questions to introduce you. Mr. Murselovic, you resided in Prijedor municipality before the war?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And even at present, you reside in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war, you were engaged in the catering and the restaurant business; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you still engage in that business?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, no, not since 1998, because after the first multi-party elections for the local assembly, I was elected the deputy president of the assembly, and in -- was elected the deputy president of the local parliament in the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is -- do you hold any position today in the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am the president of the assembly, and I'm a member of parliament in the entity called Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the party that you represent now in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I represent the party for Bosnia and Herzegovina or rather in the local elections we were together with the Party for the Integral Democratic Bosnia-Herzegovina but I'm a member of the Party for Bosnia-Herzegovina and I represent that party in the parliament of Rep -- in the entity of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Murselovic, to go back to 1992, prior to 1992, the conflict in municipality Prijedor, you were also engaged in politics; is that correct? And which party did you represent?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: In 1990, I was a member of the party of private entrepreneurs. It's a small party which brought together self-employed businessmen. Since I was one of them and since I was a member of the association of self-employed entrepreneurs, I was a member of that party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Murselovic, did you -- were you elected to the municipal assembly in Prijedor in 1990? After the multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was elected after the first multi-party elections in 1990, and at that time I became a councilman representing that party in the assembly of the municipality of Prijedor, and I was a councilman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, very quickly, in that assembly, in 1992, could you explain the representation of the members and which party members were there in the assembly and who held the majority?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: In the then assembly, the multi-party one, there were 90 seats. 30 seats were held by the Party of Democratic Action, the SDA, that is. The Serb Democratic Party, the SDS, I mean that is its acronym, had 28 seats. The Croat Democratic Union, the HDZ, had two seats. The former Socialist Party also held a number of seats. Then the so-called Reformist Forces of Ante Markovic also had a certain number of seats and I was one of the councilmen, the Socialist Alliance also had a certain number of councilmen so that all the opposition parties, if I may call them that, had 30 seats altogether, and the SDA, SDS and the HDZ had about 60 seats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Murselovic, could you explain, give the information, as to how you would -- you observed the working relationship between the main -- two main parties, the SDA and the SDS, which if I call the coalition government?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I think it had all been agreed -- it was all agreed in advance that all the small parties didn't have much say. The SDA and the SDS had the majority. They consulted each other and appeared before us with already ready-made proposals. They had a majority so it didn't really matter whether we voted yes or no, and that is how it started working from the beginning, but as the time went by, one increasingly felt that there were certain reasons, certain subjects on which they could not reach agreement so that the whole of 1991 passed in various interruptions in the work of the assembly, those two parties having failed to reach an understanding, there were frequent breaks in the work of the assembly, and that the regular parliamentary business that is decision-taking and all that was somehow pushed back to the background.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now to take your mind to the beginning of 1992, the year 1992, were you aware, and do you recall the establishment or the proclamation of the Serbian municipality that was formed in the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: In early 1992, I can't recall the exact date, it was decided, that is, there was a decision which set up this Serb Municipality of Prijedor. It looked funny to me, that is, quite simply the Serb Municipality of Prijedor was proclaimed. I found that curious because the municipality of Prijedor is one municipality, villages and people are all mixed, and I simply could not imagine how a political party could separate, step out and proclaim the Serb Municipality of Prijedor. The media then carried this announcement that the Serb Municipality of Prijedor was proclaimed, I do not know who attended that session of the assembly because we, the other councilmen were not summoned, I'm not sure any other councilmen were asked to participate in the session apart from the SDS but they held their session and they also chose all the persons who should hold all the important offices in the Serb Municipality of Prijedor from amongst the ranks of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Creation of the Serbian municipality, what did you observe with regard to the working of the members of the SDA and the SDS members in Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I have to say that members of the SDA party did not take part in that process. I do not know. But it was proclaimed -- how was it proclaimed? At a meeting at an assembly session which I said was held but I read about it in the press. They designated all the offices, all the officials and all the functions were claimed by the SDS party. Let me explain. For instance, Milomir Stakic was then the deputy president of the municipal assembly, at that assembly of the Serb Municipality of Prijedor, he was appointed the president of the assembly. Another person was designated as his deputy, for instance. Dr. Kovacevic who was the president of the executive council kept this office of the president of the executive council. For instance the President of the court was Nedzad Seric and somebody else was put in his place, Mico Kreca who was the judge in the district court in Prijedor, and it didn't sound logical to me because at that time nothing had changed yet. In point of fact, the situation on the ground was the same, but they did take this decision, proclaimed it and it was there, I suppose, in anticipation of some better times, and we were shortly to see what would happen but at that time we did not accord much importance to it. We thought that it was just a sign of some protest of one of the partners which we failed to understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as a result, did the assembly function smoothly in the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: The assembly as such did not really function smoothly. There were frequent interruptions. It was called several times in January, February, and even March, I think, but no serious work was done. And there were some understandings which we could not understand. I mean, you know what happened? Serbs would frequently -- I mean the Serb Democratic Party would frequently come up with some ultimatums to adopt a resolution to condemn this or that, or to take the decision to remain in Yugoslavia and so on. All sorts of things that were not the subject to be dealt with by the assembly of the municipality of Prijedor. Then the Serb SDS councilmen walked out of the assembly, the president of the assembly, Mr. Muhamed Cehajic then adjourned the session so that there were several attempts to go on working but the assembly simply did not function.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, moving on, you are aware that there was a change of -- in power in the municipality of Prijedor on the 30th of April, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this takeover, after the 30th of April, 1992, could you briefly explain and state what political changes that you saw in the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of April, or rather the next morning, I got up and I could see that the streets were swarming with soldiers, that at all the junctions and at all the crossings there were some checkpoints with the military and the radio began to air a proclamation and there were posters all over the town with the text of this proclamation, saying that the Serb Democratic Party had taken -- had taken over the power in the municipality of Prijedor because it could no longer bear, it could no longer watch the municipality of Prijedor go down the drain, both economically and politically, that this was the necessary step and that that was why the SDS had taken over the power. So these posters were all around the streets and it was signed by the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Prijedor and that was the first time that we came face to face with that. I must say that it all came as a surprise to us. A day or two later, the curfew was introduced from 10.00 in the evening until 6.00 in the morning and generally speaking, there was noticeably larger presence of both the military and the police. True, I need to add that we heard this repeated over and over again, that the SDS had taken over the power without a single bullet fired, and they were justifying their action by saying they wanted to save the town from the chaos, political and all the rest. However, I must say that the situation changed radically, the curfew -- well, I observed it and I didn't go out after 10.00 in the evening so people locked themselves up in their houses, in daytime there was -- you could feel there was fear there. At that time, also, Serb soldiers or rather the Territorial Defence went to Slavonia, to Pakrac, to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Lipik in Croatia, I mean, they would come back so there would be gunfire all night long and people began to be afraid, began to feel insecure, uncertain, as to the future. Naturally, after they took over the power, the assembly did not meet again, at least not in the form in which it was elected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, you referred to the Crisis Staff. Did you know who were the members who were in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've said that it became clear to us only then it became clear to us that that Crisis Staff, as far as we could see, and this was what we were convinced of, from the Serbian municipality of Prijedor, so to speak, that president who had been appointed, Milomir Stakic, as the deputy president, he had been appointed as president, and he became the president of the Crisis Staff. So he was deputy president of the municipality and became The president of the municipality and became the president of the Crisis Staff. Instead of the chief of the police who was a Bosniak up until then, all of a sudden, a new chief of the police appeared on the scene who had been appointed in the Serbian municipality of Prijedor as the chief of police, Simo Drljaca, as president of the Court there was Mr. Kreca. He was appointed as I said a minute ago. Instead of the secretariat for national defence, Medunjanin was appointed there before, someone else was appointed instead of him, a Serb, et cetera, et cetera. So all those who were appointed in that Serbian municipality of Prijedor, they took over these posts and in a certain sense they became the leaders in that Serbian municipality of Prijedor and we identified that with the Crisis Staff, because the Crisis Staff and Mr. Milomir Stakic often explained themselves after the proclamation and they -- he clearly declared himself as the president of the Crisis Staff and of the assembly at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, talking about the Crisis Staff, the people who were in the Crisis Staff, were there any, according to your information and knowledge, were there any military personnel in the Crisis Staff in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was one man who introduced himself as the chief of the Territorial Defence and he would often go to Pakrac, Lipik. He was a -- someone who wasn't a professional soldier. Mr. Slobodan Kuruzovic was his name. Apart from that the chief of the garrison, it was someone -- I don't know what his rank was. His name was Mr. Zeljaja and there was a Mr. Radmilo Arsic, I think his first name was Radmilo, yes. They were members of the Yugoslav army and they held certain positions. I don't know what rank they had, Major, Colonel, I don't know, in the garrison in the municipality of Prijedor and they became part of that Crisis Staff. And after certain incidents, they would often speak, issue certain ultimatums that had to do with the surrendering of weapons and with all the subsequent events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Murselovic, after the takeover on the 30th of April, 1992, you testified previously with regard to a meeting with the President of the Crisis Staff, Mr. Milomir Stakic, a few days after the takeover. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Mr. Stakic was the deputy president of the municipality and we would often see each other at the assemblies, at the sessions of the assemblies. He was even a guest in some of my restaurants at the time, and when that happened, when he became the leading man in a certain sense and when all the Bosniaks were sent back from their jobs and no one was allowed to enter the municipality or the organs of administration or into the court, we talked about that day at length when power was taken over and when Mr. Nedzad Seric, who was the president of the court, he was sent back from the entrance, we were shocked by this when we found out about that. Mr. Seric was a respected man from Prijedor. He was the president of the court and even the women, the officials, they talked about this, they said, "can you imagine this? They sent Mr. Seric back from the door." He was the president of the court. It was unusual for us. And when Mr. Stakic took over, to turn back to that subject, I was very interested in what that meant. In the sense of how things had changed. I was the president of independent entrepreneurs and I wanted to find out whether we would be working at all, whether it had sense for our catering establishments to work, et cetera. I wanted to know whether people would be able to continue to work or whether something unusual would happen. So I told the President's secretary I would be coming to visit, so Mr. Stakic's secretary, who was then promoted to the position of president, and I wanted to talk to him, I wanted to find out what was at issue, what was happening. I was accompanied by a transport man, someone called Pavicic, a secretary from our association, Mr. Simatovic, he was a Serb, the other one was a Croat and there was another person who was a Bosniak. He was with me too and he also -- he was also involved in the catering industry and in certain other businesses. Mr. Stakic saw us, as soon as we entered the hall that was a little before 10.00 in the morning, I saw that the secretary who had been working up until then for Mr. Cehajic, I saw that she was there and that she was still working there. And in the municipality of Prijedor, there is an office, a reception area, and on one side you have the president's office and the deputy president's office on the other. That's how it's been for 30 or 40 years in the municipality. I noticed that Mr. Stakic had already moved into the office which had -- which was for the president of the assembly. The offices are the same size but one is connected to a room because of meetings, et cetera, that was the custom. I joked with that secretary, with Mica because we had known each other for a long time and I said, "My dear Mica, these people are changing all the time but you're a permanent element here. You know." And she laughed. So then we went to see Stakic together. He saw us. A gentleman went out of his office, came out of his office. He is a councilman now, Mr. Marko Pavic. Before he was also the president of the assembly. He had the last mandate in the so-called socialist system and Stakic was quite pleasant. He saw us in. I said these are my colleagues from the association. If the work of political parties is forbidden does that mean that the associations of entrepreneurs, that their work is also forbidden? What does this all mean? And he told me, "well, to tell you the truth, Muso," that's how they called me, "I don't know what to tell you. I'm now getting ready to go to Banja Luka. I've got to go to Banja Luka at 10.00 and when I return, I'll explain everything to you. I'll have more information and I'll tell you whether you'll be able to work." There were shortages, very often there wasn't any petrol, et cetera. We had a lot of problems. It was difficult for us to work and I told him what our problems were and I asked him to tell us what this meant for the future, whether something would be changed, if the political power structure had been changed did that mean that the economy would function, does it mean that these private enterprises will work, et cetera, but he spoke about totally different issues, as far as I can remember. He mentioned certain things which at the time I have to say I didn't understand very well. He said that in Kupres, certain things were happening, I don't know what and we wondered whether we would be working. Something like that. But in any event he told me, you know, "I'm going to Banja Luka. I'm in a hurry now, I'll find out everything that I need to know over there. I'll get the information and when I return in a day or two days' time, I'll call you and then I'll tell you what will happen." We didn't spend more than ten minutes there. We said goodbye to each other. I saw that he was in a hurry. We left. I think that he was correct when he saw us. But he didn't contact me afterwards. We didn't see each other afterwards. And he didn't contact me either. Things unfolded in a completely different way. So we didn't see each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, why do you think Mr. Stakic said he was going to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, look, the Autonomous Region of Banja Luka had been proclaimed then and before that, some sort of normal reorganisation so to speak, of the entire system of working, et cetera. Before that, sometime before that, there were certain changes in the payment of taxes and contributions and there was the proclamation of these autonomous regions and he quite simply thought that he was going to consult someone there to see how that would function in the future, et cetera. So that's what I understood him to be saying and that's in fact what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, moving on to the month of May, 1992, you testified in the Stakic trial in detail with regard to the incident that took place on the 22nd of May, 1992, in Hambarine. After that, thereafter, do you recall any shelling of Hambarine and what took place in that area?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that that was a -- throughout the month of May, that was a time when there were many incidents, quite a lot of -- the population was disturbed quite a lot. There was a lot of shooting, there were a lot of uniforms around town. There were drunken soldiers walking around town. They were bearing arms, et cetera. There was an incident in Hambarine. What exactly happened, we were only able to find this out through the proclamations, through announcements from the Crisis Staff. They alone communicated with the population through the media. Perhaps if some members of the Crisis Staff provided an explanation. What was at issue, in fact, there was some sort of shooting at a checkpoint in Hambarine and I think that this resulted in the death of one of the Serbian soldiers, one of the Serbian soldiers was killed, someone who wanted to pass through the checkpoint in Hambarine. I have to say that Hambarine is an enclave which consisted of six local communes. The population was Bosniak, Muslim, purely Bosniak and Muslim, so when some soldiers wanted to pass through, soldiers from the Territorial Defence units, Bosniaks stopped them and shooting broke out. One of the soldiers who was in the -- in a car, a Serbian soldier, I think one was killed, one was wounded, something like that. The Crisis Staff then made an announcement, naturally, according to which all members of the Territorial Defence had to surrender their weapons. They said the perpetrator should be handed over. There are various versions of what happened in Hambarine, but they insisted on the weapons being surrendered. And on the perpetrators surrendering themselves to the Crisis Staff. I think that Radmilo Zeljaja also made such announcements, they were all involved in these negotiations that had to do with surrendering weapons, et cetera. But the Bosniaks didn't want to surrender their weapons. And then I think that was on the 23rd or the 22nd, I don't know exactly, a day or two later, Hambarine was shelled. It was shelled from all directions. I think there were heavy weapons around Prijedor and at certain checkpoints above Prijedor at that time and then that village was shelled indiscriminately. One or two tanks even passed through the town. They arrived below Hambarine and they fired at each house. I think the shelling was quite indiscriminate and quite a lot of civilians died then. But they still kept repeating that they would disarm the units of the Territorial Defence et cetera. So that was the shelling. I didn't go up there at the time. I didn't have any contacts but I know that there were quite a few wounded people and quite a few people who were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, before we go to the area with regard to where you would speak about your arrest, do you recall the shelling of Kozarac on the 24th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was a day or two later. Kozarac is on one side of Prijedor and Hambarine is on a completely different side of Prijedor, in fact. Kozarac is to the east of Prijedor and Hambarine more to the west. Requests were made there for weapons to be surrendered too and I was later informed that certain conflicts broke out, they asked for the policemen to surrender, they asked for the police to be disarmed and the Bosniaks in Kozarac, and at that point Kozarac was also shelled. It's the first time I saw how these heavy weapons fired over the town at Kozarac and there were some firing from the immediate vicinity. That was my first experience, the first time I saw a real war in the sense of the artillery being used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, you were arrested on the 23rd of May, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was Saturday, the 23rd of May. The curfew was still in force, people didn't go out. They remained at home for the most part. I have to say that at the time I watched the news at 7.00 and I have to say I was sitting in my office in the centre of town, in the main street. The only news programme that was watched was the Banja Luka news because the repeaters on Kozara had been destroyed earlier on, the transmitters had been destroyed, so we only watched the news at 7.00. The news that was broadcast from Banja Luka. That was that autonomous region, I don't know how it was organised. But there was only a news programme at 7.00. We couldn't watch the Sarajevo or Zagreb news or the Belgrade news. Only the Banja Luka news programme at 7.00. Because usually, the news was at half past 7.00 but this was at 7.00. I was sitting there and I watched the news and at one point the speaker said something like this: "A group of extremists from Kozarac has confessed, as admitted that the financing was provided by a well known catering person from Prijedor, Muharem Murselovic that weapons were financed," something like that, certain other names were mentioned, someone called Kulenovic from Zagreb, someone else. People I don't know. I was surprised by this news, and as I was sitting in my office I phoned the police immediately and I remember that a policeman called Jankovic picked up the phone. And I asked him, "What's going on? What do you mean financing? You know we were in a situation we were like mice in the town. What's this all about? This really wasn't the truth, you know." And he told me, "I don't know about that. I haven't got a clue." I asked had him is there anyone who can deny this? Is there anyone who could say that this has nothing to do with the truth? And he said, "I don't know. If necessary, someone will call you." I don't remember whether I later went to see him, since it wasn't far. I was about 100 metres -- it was about 100 metres away from my flat. That was the distance between my flat and the police station. There was just the park and a hotel between us, in fact. I returned -- I was in my office again, and half an hour later, someone called me from the street. I opened the window. I saw two policemen there. One of them -- I knew one of them. His name was Bato Kovacevic. Perhaps that was his nickname. Maybe it's Slobodan. But Kovacevic is his surname for sure. He said, "Come out, they need to see you in the police station." I said, "Well, I've just been there, I just called them. I can't remember." He said, "No, come on, they want to see you." I went out. The policeman I didn't know -- I don't know his name in fact -- asked me whether I had any weapons. I said I've got some kind of a pistol up there in the safe. I don't know. He said, "Okay, let's go to the police station." They took me into an office. I think there were 32 or 33 offices on the first floor -- I think it was office 32 or 33 on the first floor, and one young man called Krneta questioned me. A young man. He took a blank sheet of paper, wrote my name and surname down, my date of birth, the name of my father, of my mother, my mother's maiden name, and he asked me what I knew about that affair. I said, "I know what you know. The same things that you know. I heard this piece of information and I phoned you. What's going on? This has to be denied. We need to know the truth." So we were there from 8, 9, 10.00 he said he was married no a Muslim he had recently become a father. He was a modest man, a young man, a nice man. He didn't say anything. I said, "What am I going to do here? Am I going to spend the night here? Are you going to let me go home? It's 11.00, what's going on. No one tells me anything." He said you'll spend the night here. I asked him, "Am I arrested?" And he said, "well." So at about 11.00 they took me out of the hall. Behind me I saw a colleague of mine. Music Ilijaz. He was a professor and at one time we worked together at the catering school. Ilijaz Music. We waved to each other. They took us down behind the police station in Prijedor. Behind a car park. They took us into some -- into a room, where drunks and homeless people, such people, have -- go to sleep there. There was some Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sort of wooden constructions there. Soon after, Mr. Cehajic, president of the municipality, entered, and I said, "Well, this company is great." I joked. There were seven of us there. And we talked. The night was long. There were seven of us, apart from Ilijaz and Mr. Cehajic and myself, a certain Mehmet Tursic also appeared. He was the chief of the administration, of the revenue administration in Prijedor. There was a young doctor called Sikora, a Croat. And there was a tradesman I knew, Jusuf Ceric, they called him Juso. And there was a young man whom I didn't know at the time. He said he was the son of someone called Danica, who had a catering establishment. She was a Croat and her husband was a Bosniak, a Muslim, who had died earlier on in a car accident. I didn't know that Danica was a Croat but he said, "yes, my mother is a Croat." So there were the seven of us in that room. And we spent the whole night there. And throughout the night, they were taking something out in the yard. You can hear -- you could hear them operating with the weapons, take the ammunition out and shooting up into the air and they cried out all the time, "these are Ustashas, they have to be killed," et cetera, they tried to frighten us they would knock on the door a bit and so on. And as the night advanced, they -- there were some sort of bars above and occasionally a bullet would come in, would enter, we hid behind the wall on the other side. And that's where we spent the night. The following day, at 6.00 or 7.00, at dawn, they took us out, one by one, and they took us to the office for questioning. I went to see the same investigator. I was questioned there. He tried to encourage me. He said, "Well, Murselovic, you know this piece of information has been denied." I was happy. I said, "good, are you going to leave -- let me go now? What am I to do here? [Realtime transcript read in error "MS. KORNER:"] I spent the whole night in that room." He said, "I don't know anything that I can tell you about this." And that's what happened. Later on I stayed there until -- I then stayed there until 7.00 or rather in the afternoon, I was there until about 6 or half past 5.00 and then Ranko Mijic called me. He was the chief of the criminal police. Before that they brought me a beer or something to eat. The policemen had started turning up. They were moving around in the morning. And then Mico called me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We have got in the transcript appeared Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I know that. I have -- but she is everywhere, you know. So that will be corrected later. That will be corrected afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I thank my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I noticed it actually but I was going to leave it until the end. Thank you. Sorry for that interruption, sir. You may proceed but please try to cut it down a little bit. Be shorter. Because otherwise you're going to be here for a whole week.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I didn't want to disturb the witness, Your Honour. I would ask Mr. Murselovic to be brief and be short. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in actual fact, Mr. Murselovic, just to remind you, if you look at this, this is the transcript of every single word you said in Stakic. We have it. It's part of the records in this case. We are going to read it. In other words, you don't need to repeat in any great detail what you have already stated in the Stakic case. Having said that, I invite the Prosecutor to direct the witness right to what is important and the witness to be very brief in his replies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I would, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise. Somehow it all comes back to one and one starts talking about. But all I can say that around 5 or 6.00, Mr. Mijic Ranko said, "You can go now. It's been denied. But just don't leave Prijedor. And just in case, so that I went back home. And that was the end of my first arrest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, after that on the 30th of April, 1992, you were arrested for the second time; is that correct? I'm sorry, in May. On the 30th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was again arrested on the 30th of May. As a matter of fact, that day, there was a lot of shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, after that, you were taken to the Omarska camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That day, the 30th of May, I was taken away. The police came to take me. We were taken to the Balkan hotel. There were lots of people from all over. Then they put us on buses and took us to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in Omarska you were detained until the 6th of August, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Murselovic, before we ask some additional questions with regard to your detention in Omarska, I would like to ask you, you mentioned seven persons who were detained in the police station on the 23rd of May, 1992, with you, people whom you mentioned, Muhamed Cehajic, Ilijaz Music, Dr. Sikora, and the others. Did you see any of these persons after that and who are they and where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I saw some of them in Omarska, for instance, I saw Cehajic in Omarska. I saw Seric, Jusuf Seric, I saw him in Omarska. And I saw now what's his name, the director of the revenue service, oh, yes, Mehmet Tursic. Them I saw in Omarska. Those others, I never saw again and I assume or rather it can be safely assumed that they are no longer alive but those three I saw in Omarska, but in Omarska, all trace of them is lost. So that of those seven arrested, I was the only one who left Prijedor and is still alive. And the trace of those others was lost in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The persons that whom you did not see in Omarska, did you see them after the 23rd of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, never, never after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Murselovic, after you were taken to the Omarska camp, you were taken with many others in the bus, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were detained in first in the Mujo's room, the place called the Mujo's room in the restaurant building?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Dr. Muhamed Cehajic in Omarska in the Mujo's room?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cehajic, professor Cehajic, he taught in the secondary school. I saw him and he was the first person I saw in Omarska, because he was sitting in the middle of the room. And then we talked, and for about a month or two, a month, that is how long I was there, no, two months in point of fact, I used to see Mr. Cehajic except for a short time during which he was taken to Banja Luka to be interrogated but came back. But I found him in Omarska on the 30th of May when I got there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have given a detailed description of the times that you were detained in Omarska, in the previous trial. You have mentioned that -- you mentioned in the previous testimony that you were detained at the latter part before you were transferred to another camp in a place called the garage. Was there a female detained with you in that place called the garage?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: It's a double garage, about 22, 23 metres square, and with us we were about 150 or perhaps 170 in that garage, and there was one woman with us, her name was Hajra Hodzic or Hadzic, no, no, no, Hadzic, Hajra Hadzic. She was the only woman there. All the others were men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether she survived the camp or not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so because I never saw her again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other women detained in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: There were some 30-odd women there, 31, 32, I wouldn't know the exact number. They always sat in the restaurant when we ran there for our meal. Some of them were released before us. Some 7 or 8 days before we left Omarska. Others, however, stayed on and this Hajra was one of those who stayed behind and one Mahmuljin, Velida Mahmuljin, I believe, is -- her maiden name is Arnud [phoen] because I know her family, a teacher, married to late dentist, Mahmuljin, and three or four more women. Yes. Mrs. Besirevic, an economist who worked in the bank so some three or four women stayed behind I'm not sure and Hajra was one of them and all trace of them is lost since then. And those young women left earlier, I think seven or eight days earlier, they went to Trnopolje, to Prijedor, and I think they all left Prijedor later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, who were the people who were detained with you in the place called garage before you were transferred to the camp Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: With me, in the garage itself, there were many people I knew, my acquaintances from Prijedor. There was, for instance, a well known doctor, Dr. Sadikovic, Eso Sadikovic, yes, Dr. Eso Sadikovic, chief of department and a specialist for ear, nose and throat. And then there was one Sefik Terzic, nicknamed Kiki. There were lots of people in the garage and the conditions were terrible. I mean hardly a morning passed without somebody -- I mean, people frequently suffocated to death there because if you -- because there were too many people. If you pull your leg out, you can't put it back. So you just stand there because there is no -- there was no room for anything and that is how the morning comes, and when the door of the garage is opened, we all collapse, what for the lack of oxygen, what from fatigue because we spent days on end without sleeping. It was horrible. We were kept there under the pretext that we were to go for an exchange. And thank God, this did not happen because nobody ever returned who was taken for such an exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Murselovic, you mentioned the person by the name of Eso Sadikovic. Did he survive the camp? Have you met him after you were released?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, Dr. Eso, he was a popular man. Everybody liked him. He was interesting. He was good company. And he frequently wrote columns for a newspaper. He was with us in that garage. And then when we eventually left the garage, and the exchange did not take place, some three or four days later, around 10.00 at night, he was called out by a gentleman by a guard, no, not guard, Drago Prcac, an elderly policeman and he took him out around half past 10.00 or something, supposedly there was a bus ready to go somewhere, so he called out Dr. Sadikovic's name and he went out and I never saw him again so he must have been killed because he never turned up again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Murselovic, you testified in your -- the previous trial with regard to the interrogations that you faced in the Omarska camp. Did they tell you at any time as to why you were detained or why you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was interrogated by two interrogators, the name of one was Nenad Tomcic and the other one was Neso, too. All they said was, "Where -- when were you arrested? Where were you before that? Before we arrested you?" And I said, "well, where could I be? I was at home." And that was the sum of it. They asked me some other things but they never told me why I had been arrested or why I was there. I kept asking them what all this supposed to mean, whether will they let me go but they said nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, at any time did anyone institute legal action against you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: No, not against me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described in your previous testimony the occasions or the instances that you were beaten by guards in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Recalling these instances, did you at any time provoke any of the guards for them to beat you or did you do anything wrong while were you detained in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Definitely not, because we were undernourished and hungry and in rags because we had to sleep on the concrete now. A few people had some jackets or something to spread on the floor and sleep on that, or a piece of cardboard, and those fared well. Everybody was scared because people were being taken out at night and killed right in front of our eyes. So that nobody ever provoked anyone. Everybody tried to keep quiet. A man called Simo Kevic who used to work with me earlier, he said to the guards, "Well, this one persecuted Serb children whilst he was in school." So they got me and started beating me with cables and something. I know that one of those who beat me was a young man called Marmat and at some point I stopped him and I said, "ask your Borka if I ever persecuted Serb children," and then he stopped beating me and then on another occasion they beat me in the WC. I was there and they broke the door in our WC in that room where I was, all the feces was floating around so that nobody could approach it. It was very -- it was all plugged so they took me to another room to relieve myself. And as they took me there so somebody broke the door they beat with the rifle butt on the door hard, "there is a balija, he must be performing ablutions," and they broke these two ribs, and once as we were coming out carrying food, they invariably beat us and once I was well beaten up, I could not see who it was but it happened to me. So that I was beaten several times, good and proper. I don't really know why. But I wasn't the only one. They beat me just by accident without knowing or what, but some were beaten during interrogations as they were interrogated and a number of them succumbed to those beatings because their legs and arms were broken and when they would return from this interrogation, they would be in such a bad shape that they would die right there in front of us. I remember one such instance. Mr. Zijad Mahmuljin for a while he was president of the executive council he was also one of those who died amongst us and there were other such instances but I believe I've already testified about this. So that, yes, beatings were frequent. Once I -- there was Osman Mahmuljin a good friend of mine, and a doctor, he was the director of the hospital. He was with us. And I could see that those people who were beaten, they look completely changed. They had bruises and swellings on their heads and faces and all over them so we tried to put them some cold compresses to allay the pains and this doctor said, "well, I don't know, they won't last long because their kidneys have been destroyed so they will die, they will never get home." So it was really horrible to look at those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, you described about the interrogation and you referred to some of the interrogators. Do you recall these people who were referred to as interrogators as to from where they came from?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: The majority came from Prijedor. There was this one Tomcic who interrogated me, Nenad. There was also a certain Dragan Radakovic who used to be the manager of the national park and taught drawing. And there was Milo Savljevic he is at present employed in the municipal hall. There were even some from the Court. On several occasions I saw Dragan -- no, not Dragan Dragosavljevic. Dragan's son, yes, Zivko Dragosavljevic who until recently was president of the court in Prijedor. He also interrogated me. Then Tomic who was the public prosecutor he also came on several occasions. I didn't know him well at that time but he was shown to me but also there were some people whom I did not know at all. Nobody knew them because after all we knew everybody in Prijedor. So I asked who are these people? And we were told that they were from Banja Luka and they were interrogating and conducting more serious investigations. That is what Sefik Terzic told me, that they interrogated him, those interrogators from Banja Luka but they came with those interrogators from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, will this be a convenient time to take a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, certainly. Please yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will have a 25 minute break, resuming immediately thereafter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, the interpreters are finding it very difficult to catch up with the speed with which you're talking. As a result, the transcript that we are having has many, many mistakes, through no fault of the interpreters. I would kindly ask you to slow down in your answers and be as short as possible because otherwise, you will not be helping us at all. Thank you. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, before the break, you were talking about the interrogators. Now I would move your -- the area of questioning and be brief as possible when you answer the questions. Mr. Murselovic, before you were transferred to Manjaca, you testified in the previous occasion and even today that you were detained in the place called the garage, which was in the restaurant building; is that correct? And you mentioned persons such as Eso Sadikovic. Do you remember when you were transferred to Manjaca, is it correct if I say that it's the 6th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have also testified in the previous trial as to the journey from Omarska to Manjaca in your previous testimony. Now, during this journey, were the following persons -- did you know or did you see the following persons by the name of Dedo Crnalic, Nezir Krak and Djuzin, his real name being Babic? Could you briefly tell the -- explain to the Court as to what happened to these people, when you reached -- when you all reached Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: We spent the entire day of the 6th -- on the 6th of August travelling. We arrived in Omarska around 10.00 in the morning. We were taken in to Omarska and at about 10.00, we arrived at Manjaca. We stopped frequently. It was very hot. We arrived in the evening. It was dark. They left us in the bus until the following morning with the heating on, everything was shut, they didn't let us out, and then they took Dedo Crnalic out of my bus. They called out to him, asked him to come out, someone called out to him, I don't know who, they immediately started beating him. It was dark so you couldn't see much and we were lying down below the seats. After a certain time, someone threw Dedo in at the front door and that's where he remained lying. Mr. Nezir Krak wasn't in my bus. He was in the next bus. We heard him being called out. They called out to him, asked him to come out, which he did, and the following morning, when we got out of the bus, I saw that Dedo remained lying at the front door of the bus, and he didn't seem to be alive. That's what I was told. When we lined up, someone recognised that young man called Sejo Babic, his name is Sejo or Sead but everyone called him Djuzin after his older sister. Someone took him a little further away. And later on we found out that he had been killed. We were all out there standing out there, and they then started calling us out, a camp commander appeared and it was then that we realised that we had arrived at Manjaca. It was someone called Bozidar Popovic. I think that was his name. And he said, "I'm not interested in these dead people but the men who have lined up, the people who have lined up, I'll take them in." We were later informed that some of those bodies were taken to Prijedor in the buses, and Mr. Crnalic, well, his funeral was this year, in the summer, because he was floating in the Vrbas River, that someone recognised him. He was exhumed this year and buried at the local cemetery in Prijedor, whereas the others have not been exhumed yet and they haven't been found either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I have in the transcript here this year and this year. His funeral was this year in the summer because he was floating in the Vrbas River, that someone recognised him. He was exhumed this year and buried at the local cemetery in Prijedor. In other words, when was -- he was -- he was detected floating in the Vrbas River when? Soon after his arrival in Manjaca? And how did you come to know about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those dead bodies were taken back by bus and they were thrown out, they were thrown into the Vrbas River when returning. This is something that we found out later on. And somewhere near Banja Luka, I don't know where exactly, they were buried at some cemetery as unidentified persons. And there was an exhumation that took place, that was carried out this year, the family wanted Mr. Crnalic to be exhumed and he was exhumed and buried at the local cemetery in Prijedor. He was buried this year, ten years later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, how long did you stay in Manjaca? How long were you detained in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Manjaca until the 14th of November, 2002 [as interpreted], when, through the intermediary of the Red Cross, we were transferred to Karlovac, in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, you spoke about exhumations. Subsequently, after your release and after you returned to Prijedor, were you involved in the -- any exhumations that took place in the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't directly involved in that process of exhumation but I was involved in the burial of those who had been exhumed because the commission for locating missing people, the federal commission, from 1998 up until now, has been looking for missing people, and in Prijedor we've published a book of those missing. This concerns people who have disappeared without trace, who were missing, and this book of missing people from Prijedor stops at number 3.280, something like that, but the process of reporting is still ongoing, because entire families have been reported as missing or went missing, and there was no one to report this, but from 1998, and I'm referring to the commission for locating missing people, has exhumed missing people, and to date, the number of citizens, many citizens from the municipality of Prijedor have been exhumed, a lot of Bosniaks and a small number of Croats, and between 1.500 and 1.600 have been exhumed. Of this number, about 1.000 individuals have been identified, many families, many family members, have provided samples for DNA analysis so that this identification process, the process of identifying the victims, is still in progress to this very day, and I have to say that the last mass grave was found last year in the area of the iron ore mine called Jakarina Kos. That's a grave. It's thought to be a secondary grave because the bodies were transferred there from some other location. The commission for missing people and representatives of the international community exhumed about 380 bodies from that grave. And a certain number of body parts, which have nothing to do with those bodies. The burial has not taken place yet. We thought that perhaps at the end of this year or the beginning of the next year, they would be buried at local -- in local cemeteries in Prijedor and around Prijedor, in accordance with the wishes of the families. And this concerns those who have been identified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To leave the Omarska camp, during your detention what was your observation about the existence of the camp or the organisation, the day-to-day running of the camp, the Omarska camp, Mr. Murselovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the camp was very well organised. I have to say that food was brought on a daily basis -- once a day from the social catering service in Ljubija. I recognised some of them who brought the food, who were involved in that. And the camp itself was in the iron ore mine, Ljubija. The guard shift would come and the shift lasted for 12 hours. And then they were free for 24 hours after that. So we always knew which guard would be in a certain shift. This schedule wasn't changed. Every day, and regularly, on a regular basis, investigators would come, interrogators would come in a small bus. They came at about 8.00, more or less, that was in the morning, and returned between 4.00 or 5.00 or 6.00. The guard was organised, there was a guard organised in the immediate vicinity of the area -- of the premises that we were kept in and guards could also be seen a little further away. So one could safely say that this was well organised and functioned smoothly. Questions -- questioning was carried out in a certain order, certain places where the detainees were held, and on that basis, I can conclude, I can come to the conclusion, that the camp was well organised, and as soon as we arrived there on the 30th, everything was functioning. When we arrived at the Omarska camp on the 30th of May, it was already functioning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also observe dead bodies that were lying in the vicinity and subsequently they have been removed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the course of the day, someone would be killed or someone would be returned after having been questioned, would die among us, in the room we were kept in, but most of them were called out at night, the guards would call people out throughout the night and take some people away, some of those whom they had called out. And in a certain sense we never saw them alive again. In the morning, between 7.00 and 8.00, we would sometimes see near the white house on the grass, we would see people, dead people, lying on the grass and then a small van, a small yellow van, would appear. It was a small van. And it had a cabin at the front and there was -- and one part of it served for transporting freight. That's where they would load the dead bodies, five, six, or seven of them and they were taken away somewhere. That van returned perhaps about half an hour or 45 minutes later. So we came to the conclusion that it didn't go very far with its load.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, now I would take your mind to an incident, a meeting that took place in Banja Luka. Were you a member of the assembly of the Chamber of Commerce in Banja Luka before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the main commercial assembly, as it's called, and before 1990, I founded a company, as I had two catering establishments, I had 14 and 15 -- between 14 and 15 employees. I founded a company and then I don't know on whose suggestion it was, I was elected as a member of the assembly of the Chamber of Commerce in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the president of that chamber?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: The president of the Chamber of Commerce of Banja Luka was Zvonko Mersa I knew him because he was born in Sanski Most and before he came the director or rather the president of the Chamber of Commerce in Banja Luka he was the director of a big company which was called Krajinaturist and it had all catering companies under it. It unified all catering companies in the Banja Luka territory. This was some sort of organisation of -- some sort of working organisation which covered these big companies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, do you recall attending a meeting in Banja Luka where -- to elect the president for that particular year?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Zvonko's, one of his mandates had come to an end and he was put forth as a candidate by entrepreneurs to be a -- given another mandate, to be granted another mandate, and the session was scheduled, was scheduled for certain other items too but I know that one of the items had to do with electing a president of the assembly of the Chamber of Commerce in Banja Luka and Zvonko Mersa was suggested by entrepreneurs and we were members of the Chamber of Commerce. He was proposed and we were to elect him for another mandate as president.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall which year, which year it was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I think that was at the end of 1991, perhaps it was November or December, but I am almost sure that it was at the end of 1991. I don't believe that it was in 1992 because not much was happening in Prijedor at the time so I couldn't link it up to anything else but I'm almost sure it was at the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the name of the President, your nominee, was proposed, could you explain what happened during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: We were all sitting there, and all of us entrepreneurs. There were a lot of people whom I knew. And then somehow, I don't know how, Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin appeared from somewhere, two or three men were with him, and they suggested that as president of the Chamber of Commerce of Banja Luka, one of their candidates should be elected. I can't remember whom they proposed, but Mr. Brdjanin wanted to take the floor on several occasions and he insisted and he explained that the SDS was the leading party in Banja Luka. He insisted that it was necessary for someone to be a candidate and that someone should be elected following a proposal from the Serbian Democratic Party. The entrepreneurs, the private businessmen participated in the discussion. They did not share this position. And to tell you the truth, that's the first time that I saw Mr. Brdjanin. I wanted to know who that man was. I asked, "Who is this man?" They said he's an engineer from Celinac, a member of the core leadership of the SDS, et cetera. But after several discussions, we didn't accept Mr. Brdjanin's proposal. But instead, we elected the person we had proposed, Mr. Zvonko Mersa. We elected him one more time. Mr. Brdjanin left in protest with his men. That's how it ended. That's the first time I saw the gentleman. To tell you the truth, I didn't see him after that but I followed his appearances in the press. I was well informed. But after that, I did not personally see him, not until this day. Later on, when I had contact with Mr. Zvonko Mersa, I saw him at the end of 1992, beginning of 1993, in Zagreb. I met him there. I asked him what happened later on, and he said, "two or three months later, I was replaced." But I've also seen Mr. Zvonko in Sanski Most and in Zagreb recently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Murselovic, do you recall in the -- during the Stakic trial, you presented the Trial Chamber with a document which was subsequently admitted as an exhibit, which you had in your possession? Do you recall that instance?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be permitted to give this document to Mr. Murselovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Which in the Stakic trial had the exhibit number 45A. And in this trial, which is, I'm told, which is numbered at P255. And the other document which has the Stakic number as Exhibit S45-1A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, can we put the English text on the ELMO? Okay. Yes, question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document? Did you see this document before?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber as to how -- when you saw this document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I saw this document after the war. An acquaintance, a Serb acquaintance of mine, brought this document to me. It had to do with Mr. Stakic, because on the other side, there was Mr. Stakic's signature, and this decision, signed by Mr. Brdjanin on the other side was endorsed, I can't remember what it said, but there was a signature, president of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Prijedor, Mr. Milomir Stakic. It was then that I saw this text of this decision which was signed by Mr. Brdjanin, and I have its copy before me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be permitted to show Exhibit S -- Stakic number -- case number S46B, ERN number 00633171?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, is that the document that you were speaking about, that you presented to the Trial Chamber in the Stakic case?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have the English translation of the same document, which in the Stakic case was Exhibit S46A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Which could be put on the ELMO. Thank you, Your Honour. May I be -- I'm told that an exhibit number should be given to these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a double reference number in one. Basically, I think it would be P154 something/ and then the Stakic exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: May I read it as P1542/ --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: S46A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the last one that we have seen. The previous ones will be -- now, let's start, P1542/45A will be the first of the documents that you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With the Serbo-Croat or Serbian version in Cyrillic becoming /S45B.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then what was in Stakic, S45-1A becomes P1543/S45-1A.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: It should be P1542.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're keeping 1542?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: As it's the same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I can live with that. No problem. And then the next one, then there is of course the Cyrillic text which will be /S45-1B, all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then S 46 A becomes P1542/S46A and B. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Please bear with me, Your Honour. The transcript number being P1542.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then /S46A and then /S46B and then there is another one which is identical to the last one in Serbo-Croat which is S46-1B.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, sorry for interrupting you. I don't want to take any of your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Referring to the document which is signed by the president, Radoslav Brdjanin, could you read the heading of that document, Mr. Murselovic, please? That's 45A.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: The document is headed "decision" and then it says the letterhead or rather the number and the date, and then, "Decision." This is called decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the document speaks for itself, I don't want you to read out the document. How did you get this document? When did you first see this document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I saw this document when a citizen of Prijedor, and it was sometime in the year 2000 or 2001, brought this document to me, to my office. We talked about something and he asked me if I had seen this decision. Well, I had some idea. There was a lot of talk about the existence of such decisions but I'd never seen one before, and then he showed it to me and told me, "Well, you can keep it if you want to." And I took it. On one side, was this decision made by the Banja Luka Crisis Staff and signed by Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin, and on the other, on the verso, was not the decision but Mr. Milomir Stakic was signed there and there were closely related, that is, on the same sheet of paper but on the verso side, that had Mr. Stakic's signature and the letterhead and the seal of the municipality of Prijedor, and the decision of Milomir Stakic, rather, and this Mr. Stakic's decision has to do with a decision which was signed by Mr. Brdjanin, and it's date is only one day later. That is, that document, the decision is the -- dated the 22nd of June and Mr. Stakic's document is dated one day later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes the examination, as I'm new to the procedure in this Trial Chamber, do I submit the exhibits at this stage or at the end?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No I would prefer if you would submit the exhibits at this stage straight away so that we can facilitate matters. If you want some time, perhaps we could start with the cross-examination and you can do that. If you're ready, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender it but the documents would be ready at the next session, after the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. All right. So we will do that Ms. Gustin, in due course. Take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Murselovic, you are going to be cross-examined now by Mr. Trbojevic, who I suppose you know, and he is co-counsel with Mr. Ackerman on the Defence team for Mr. Brdjanin. Mr. Trbojevic, the witness is all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not have too many questions. Should we perhaps make a break now or what? I don't think I will take more than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you are in a position, because we have three-quarters of an hour for the next break so if you are in a position to start with your cross-examination, start now and finish when you finish. I mean no one is chasing you. You take your time. If instead you require a short break, I can give you a short break too. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. No, I do not need any special break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Please do not feel constrained that you need to finish the cross-examination by a particular time. Take your time. The day is all yours. We don't have another witness this morning, no? So --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No we do not have any witness for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Richterova. Mr. Trbojevic, cross-examination. Cross-examined by Mr. Trbojevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
