utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Murselovic. You already gave long and exhaustive answers but nevertheless, my job is to ask you some more questions, perhaps we shall need some further clarifications.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please speak into his microphone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My attention is being drawn that you need to move the microphone a little bit and speak straight into it because the interpreters are having some difficulties. Yes, and one other thing, Mr. Murselovic, and Mr. Trbojevic, Mr. Trbojevic is very familiar with this already but probably you're not, since you both speak the same language, there is always the tendency that one doesn't wait before putting a new question or answering a question. So please allow a short interval between question and answer and vice versa so that you do not cause difficulties to the interpreters. Mr. Trbojevic, sorry for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So following the multi-party elections, a coalition of national -- of ethnic parties formed the government and took their seats in the assembly and it more or less was in proper working order in 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. It worked. There was a semblance of work, because they managed to divide between themselves the chief offices, that is the assembly met but there were many problems and interruptions and recesses and so on and so forth but yes, you could say that it worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the general political situation in the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had, to all intents and purposes, drastically changed following this multi-party elections over the next year or so, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a war in Croatia. The then Yugoslav army and members of reserve units, of the Yugoslav army went to the front in Croatia. The units from Prijedor went to Lipik, to Slavonia generally speaking, to that area so that that was a time which was wartime, to call it that. And in Prijedor, you could sense it because somehow there was insecurity, there were shots fired, there was intimidation and so on and so forth. So, well, yes, the assembly met but one could say its performance was not particularly high.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you were a politician and you were a councilman, I'd like to draw on your experience, of your knowledge of the circumstances then, and will you tell us, isn't it true that the Presidency of the former SFRY had also broken apart and the federal assembly too? It also was paralysed, it couldn't work?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Presidency of Yugoslavia, we are now somewhere in the higher political spheres, at that time it had still not broken apart, but there were constantly some problems. It was a time when that Presidency still worked, it still worked. And it was a time when those representatives we had, that is representatives of the then republics, travelled from one part of Yugoslavia to another in pursuit of a solution for the future of Yugoslavia, seeking pursuit of a solution that would permit Yugoslavia to survive. And that was the principal stumbling block because they somehow could not see eye to eye. Some republics openly said that they wanted to walk out of the federal state of Yugoslavia. Some fought to preserve that state. And that was that time. And in the meantime, in the latter half of 1991, war broke out in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the former constitution of the SFRY was still in force?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: The constitution did not change. It could not be changed under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the role of the Yugoslav People's Army was to preserve the territorial integrity and viability of the territory?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: That is what the constitution said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this actions which this army undertook in Slovenia and Croatia were aimed at trying to preserve the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia. And that was in accordance with the constitution, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you how I see those things. After those first incidents in Slovenia and you must remember them, the television made a big deal of that, when a Bosnian soldier said, "Well, we are allegedly attacking, they are allegedly defending themselves." Remember that? Then it became already obvious that the situation was not -- would not remain and that the policy that is some Serbian politicians were already saying that they wanted to preserve the ethnic areas where in their opinion the Serbs lived, and under the circumstances, naturally, the Yugoslav People's Army was of two minds, if I may put it that way. That is at that time, members of other ethnic groups began to leave the Yugoslav People's Army. Immediately after the start of the conflict in Croatia, in 1991, the Yugoslav People's Army was, if I may put it that way, cleansed of the members of other ethnic groups and we all believed, if Croatia was gone,, that is, if Slovenia was gone and if Croatia refused to be in this association of states, then we thought that there was no room for Bosnia-Herzegovina in such an union, because the Serb people was predominant and then the army and all the other structures would then predominate too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if we say that these are the -- that this is the source of the coalition partners in the municipal assembly in Prijedor, you will agree with that, I hope, won't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I could say that these were opinions which could not be harmonised. Those were two different opinions and there was no meeting point with them. Our municipal assembly was asked, and I have to say that for the sake of truth, that is the Serb Democratic Party requested the municipal assembly to adopt something like a declaration, something like a decision, stating that we wanted to stay in Yugoslavia, that is to say, lend our support to this whole process. The SDA could not agree with that. We could not agree, we could not go along with that because I thought then and I think that today, that Yugoslavia could not exist or cannot exist without Slovenia, without Croatia, and to my mind, that is not Yugoslavia any longer. And by the very fact that in 1918, when Yugoslavia was founded, as the kingdom of the Serbs, Croats and Slovenes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we don't have to go so far back. Wouldn't you agree --

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree but we could not accept that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I hope you won't hold it against me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these were insurmountable differences and what it led to was to report to the -- respond to the callout or not, this was another difference between the SDA and the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember a case which started at that time -- I can't even tell you when exactly because I don't have these documents with me -- that in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that multi-party one, had embarked on the debate on the protection of the vital national interests? It was in the wake of the constitution of the assembly, in the wake of the oath they took, and they were saying that they were to prepare the text of the new constitution so when the problem of the protection of the vital national interests would come up, then certain procedure would be set in place, events would be organised and so on and so forth, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That is what we have now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course, it all ended when the war broke out, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let's go back to the situation in the municipality. Soldiers are coming back from the front, bringing their weapons with them, so of course some are afraid, some are shocked, some feel very powerful and all sorts of things happen in the town. You told us about that. Is it true that, economically speaking, when payments were interrupted with Slovenia and Croatia when the war broke out, when it became difficult to do business with Yugoslavia, that the situation, that the businesses -- that the economy was disrupted?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. You mentioned a detail. When people came back from the front, at that time, we still tended to idealise things. I remember a detail when Mr. Kuruzovic, Slobodan Kuruzovic brought a car for himself from Croatia, and many other things were brought over. Among other things, he brought another car, a car for himself, a good car for him, from Croatia, and we simply couldn't understand that there was all this looting, and why all this was being done, and under what excuse did he bring in this car? Besides, everything was disrupted, inflation was rampant, and somebody persistently offered this money, those dinars, which were dinars which were exchanged in the streets and the inflation was going up from one day to the other, and people would change as much money as they needed until noon and afternoon one had to change more money because the dinar would lose some of its value. So the economic situation was nothing to write home about. But there was a lot of speculation that this money was being brought in by the troops, and that the army trucks were used to bring in this money and that it was being sold in order to get healthy, sound illegal currency back. That's the German marks. So that salaries were not worth anything and companies could not work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And naturally people were absent, they were off to the front, they were not at their workplaces?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, and there were shortages of everything, of fuel, raw materials, and I also have to say that Bosniaks and Croats refused to respond to the call-ups, and they were other requests to hand over weapons. Weapons were handed over, but what people found particularly hard was when they came back from the front and they came back through Gradiska, Banja Luka and Prijedor, that was the route they took, throughout, I don't know how many weapons there were, but there was talk that one could not walk through Prijedor really, because the town was all littered with cartridges and empty shells and whatnot and every night there would be shooting, so that there was this -- people felt very insecure. So that was a time fear and insecurity was very characteristic -- the principal characteristics of that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, there is some information that the weaponry that belonged to the Territorial Defence was distributed among the people in 1991, that it went out on to the ground?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have such information, and I do not know who it was distributed to but what I do know is that Serb villages were being intensively armed and they had weapons, whereas the Bosniaks did not have weapons, but they frequently bought weapons with all that fear around. Somebody was selling something. I have to tell you something. Soldiers coming back from the front used to sell their weapons. I don't know how they were allowed to bring them there. So that a neighbour of mine said, "Murselovic, mind you don't buy a weapon from a Serb soldier because he'll take your money but he will then report the number of the weapon he sold." And I recently saw this man, it's another matter that I never intended to buy any weapon but no doubt it was very well organised, that somebody was to sell weapons to the Bosniaks, and then he was duty-bound to keep the money but report the number of that weapon to somebody, and that person then, when requesting that the weapons be handed over because there was this action: "Turn over your weapons, turn over your weapons," but it concerned only the Bosniaks and Croats, you know the Serbs did not have to return the weapons because they were mobilised so that they knew in advance who had weapons and people had sooner or later to return those weapons and then it will be established that it was this rifle, the number so and so, such and such, so that there were all sorts of things going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any activity with regard to those weapons? Did they try to prevent its illegal distribution?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were attempts that were made. The first incident occurred when the Bosniaks returned those weapons, the Bosniaks and Croats returned the weapons in front of the municipality. They didn't want to go to the line and they left the weapons there. There was -- there were a lot of people there. They tried to find a common language to reach an agreement but I, to tell you the truth, didn't participate in that. I believe that it was best for me to see as little as possible and to know as little as possible. I was a councilman and I didn't participate in the authorities. I wasn't part of the authorities so I didn't want to meddle in that affair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did you hear that some of the Serbian soldiers lost his job or they lost their job because they didn't respond to the mobilisation, they didn't respond to the call-up?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps there were -- there was one case or perhaps there were two cases I couldn't count the number of cases on my fingers. I couldn't say how many Serbs didn't want to respond to the mobilisation. There were very few such cases. Perhaps they tried to avoid being mobilised by some other means, you know. But what is for sure is that there were very few such cases because all the time, a propaganda war was being conducted, which stated that the Serbs were under threat and that they had to defend themselves, et cetera. They were told that 1941 should not be repeated but there were few men. Later I was told that some people had left, had gone to Belgrade, there were such cases but the vast majority took up arms and went to the front, to Croatia. There is something else I would like to say. The local papers at the time kept reporting on this and films were shown from the battlefield, and it was then that I first heard the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. term mopping up, you know, that was something that was ugly and that two pages in the Kozarski Vjesnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because you're not answering the question. You're deviating from the question which was a very a simple one: "Tell me did you hear that some of the Serb soldiers lost their job, et cetera" and you answered, "yes there may have been one or two cases" and that should have been the end of your answer. Next question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you agree with me that that was legally a possibility, that it was a legal possibility that they could be held responsible, legal proceedings could be instituted against them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that from the 30th of April, when the Serbian Democratic Party proclaimed that power had been taken over, you said from that time on, all the leaders and prominent people of other nationalities were replaced?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then workers too?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we agree that from the 30th of April onwards, up until the 22nd of July, which is -- the 22nd of July, which is the date of the decision that you looked at, most replacements of personnel had been carried out in the course of April and May and those three weeks in June?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, most of the leaders had been sent back, had been sent back from their work, and in the meantime some of them had been taken to camps, and they didn't go to work at all. I think that this decision established the situation on the ground, you know. The actual situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, tell me, they spoke about -- there was discussion about the appointment of the chief of police and you expanded on this in response to a question put to you by the defence in the Stakic case and I wouldn't want to go into that discussion at the moment but we are in a dilemma. The chief of police in the municipality is to be appointed by the minister of the interior, according to the law. You said that the municipality had something to say and either had to agree to something or propose something?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: To propose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know but could we expand on that and provide an additional clarification about the law, the law says that the chief of police in municipalities is to be appointed by the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct but the appointment is very often just formal. The assembly appoints someone in accordance with proposals from certain structures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The minister of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you didn't know whether the chief of police had to report to the executive board of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know but I think that cooperation was quite close because when Mr. Simo Drljaca was appointed, he was appointed in the Serbian municipality of Prijedor as the chief of the police too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you about this propaganda, something about this propaganda. And you have said something about that on page 4 of your testimony of December, 1997, that's the first statement, the date of which is incorrect, it says 1992. On page 4, you said that that propaganda wasn't directly against non-Serbs but that Muslims were accused for not participating in the fight against the Ustasha and they complained about events that took place in 1941 et cetera. Is there anything else that we could say about that propaganda?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, there was a propaganda war which was conducted with a lot of insistence, they said that the Serbs were in danger and that one shouldn't allow 1941 to happen again. And secondly, there was constant propaganda in the sense that some of the Bosniaks apparently killed a Serbian friend and then they said that there was an event, Dr. Osman Mahmuljin was supposed to kill a colleague of his, a doctor who was ill, et cetera. We knew that this was falsehood, that people from Stubice had to kill their neighbours and there were certain list that were circulating, you know. I'm sure that none of that was true. And that someone was planting such stories and encouraging such things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke to Stakic a day or two after the 30th of April, you said that one of the questions that you put to him was whether political parties had been prohibited?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that question have a cause? Was there an announcement according to which the parties had been prohibited?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as soon as there is an announcement they say that in a multi-party system, one party is taking over power, as soon as there is such a proclamation then it's obvious that one, other parties are prohibited because they used force to take over power. And in that announcement, everything was directed against the SDA, but among other things I was told -- I asked what does that mean? Is work forbidden? Is the parliament going to function? I was interested in how this would be functioning. I said if this is going to be prohibited, can we work through the association? Will private enterprises be able to work? Will we be able to get petrol, will shops be able to work, will anything function? That's what I was thinking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to check whether there was an announcement according to which work was prohibited?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Stakic, while you discussed this matter, how are we going to work, whether we will work, he mentioned the situation in Kupres, that something was happening in Kupres, what did that have to do?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he said that people over there were more or less fighting already and that everyone had been mobilised. And that we hadn't yet felt those terrible consequences of the war, that's what I thought he was referring to. I didn't assume that that would happen in our locality in a couple of days. He mentioned Kupres, and at the time I didn't understand, because I have to say that at the time we were in a situation where there was a classical blockade, an absolute media blockade so we didn't know what was happening anywhere. As I said a minute ago, all the transmitters had already been destroyed. The transmitter on Kozara was not working and we could only watch Banja Luka television. I don't know what it was called at the time. And we could listen to the local radio station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, a lot of information about what was happening in Kupres was not available to you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, with regard to this event in Hambarine and in Kozarac, you said there was an incident in Hambarine and, if I'm not mistaken, you said one person was wounded and another person was killed, there was certain other information but that is not important right now, what I'm interested in is was there an incident that preceded the situation in Kozarac? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, before that, in Kozarac, the entire police force was disarmed, and I'm referring to the police from the -- the police force from Kozarac, and I have to say that the policemen who were Bosniaks, we still haven't exhumed them but they were disarmed and the army took over. The Territorial Defence in Kozarac, in a certain sense, they blocked Kozarac, they put up checkpoints of their own, but people kept passing through towards Brajkovac through Kozarac and I know that people from Kozarac said that there were quite a few provocations from the police on the way to Kozarac. I don't know, they had put obstacles in front of cars, et cetera. There were these minor provocations, you know, the ones that we are good at. So a request was made for Kozarac to be disarmed and a conflict broke out. There was a direct conflict. What happened after that, I don't know, because Kozarac is 12 kilometres from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Hambarine and in Kozarac, there were ultimatums, requests for the weapons to be surrendered and for perpetrators to surrender themselves, as you said?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that one ultimatum was signed by the Crisis Staff and today you said that one ultimatum was signed by Radmilo Zeljaja?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: That's incorrect, Your Honour, if I may recall, remember, it was not said that it was signed by the Crisis Staff, and it was signed by Radmilo Zeljaja, that it was announced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right actually. Yes, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the same to me. I didn't literally mean a signature on a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's put the question to the witness or the statement to the witness as corrected by Mr. Waidyaratne. Do I pronounce your name well? Because I find it difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, very correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One ultimatum was announced by the Crisis Staff and another by Radmilo Zeljaja or the command?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that they were together, Radmilo Zeljaja as commander of the army was also part of the Crisis Staff, as such he represented so to speak the military part of that entire process. We identified the two with each other because in Kozarac, an open conflict broke out. After the shelling of Kozarac, there were -- there was fighting on a large scale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of the day, I understood you -- I thought that you said that there were various ultimatums but now you're saying that this included the one and the other?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, an ultimatum means that there has to be an unconditional surrender of weapons, the perpetrators have to surrender unconditionally, individuals have to surrender unconditionally, weapons, too. That's an ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to determine how many of them participated in that. On page 4 of your statement, dated the 13th of January of this year, you said that you thought that the coordination between the Crisis Staff and the military command was absolute. You said that the Crisis Staff had both military and civilian power and in the same paragraph, you said that the army had its own command hierarchy so these two things seem to contradict, there seems to be a contradiction here.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: In the Crisis Staff, Mr. Kuruzovic was in the Crisis Staff. He had the rank of major. I know him personally. I don't know these military men. He went to the battlefield in Slavonia, in Croatia. Mr. Zeljaja was there and he participated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you're answering the question. The question was this it's being put to you that in the same context you first affirmed that the Crisis Staff had a both military and civilian power and also that there was a hierarchy, command hierarchy, inside the army. Mr. Trbojevic thinks or believes that those two statements are conflicting. Would you agree to that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think they -- there was very close cooperation between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that when you were arrested the second time, you said you were taken away and you wanted to ask them where they were taking you and one JNA soldier, you said, pointed a pistol at you. That was on the 30th of May. I believe that you heard that the JNA had officially withdrawn its units from Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 19th of May. So could this be a JNA soldier or was this soldier a member of the Army of Republika Srpska, of some second or third unit?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I said that he was wearing a JNA uniform, a JNA military uniform. I don't see much of a difference here. You know the ranks and everything is the same. They wear the same uniform and there are no particular insignia that can enable one to distinguish them from others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One would expect that the JNA soldier had JNA insignia on him. There would be the five-corner star?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't have a cap.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ordinary soldiers didn't have pistols as part of the standard weapons issued to them. So if he didn't have a cap, he wasn't wearing regulation uniforms. If he doesn't have a regular weapon he's not a regular soldier. He doesn't seem to be a regular soldier.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I got off the bus, I crossed the Zeger crossing and went in the direction of the police station. A man approached me. I didn't know him. He was in a military uniform and he asked me, "Where are you going?" I told him why I wanted to go to the police station. I said, "We didn't know where we were going or why we were going there." But when I told him my name, he took a pistol out and said, "You want to cut throats of Serbian children." He kicked me and I immediately got into the bus. I didn't have much time to observe what sort of insignia he had or what his rank was because I entered the bus and I lay down on my stomach.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me in response to a question from the Prosecution, you said that while you were in Omarska, they -- no proceedings were instituted against you. I think that you said no proceedings were instituted against me. Were any proceedings instituted against anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: We spoke to each other. We spoke amongst ourselves and we would usually ask each other, what had happened, what did they ask you about, et cetera. That's quite normal. Some said that they had signed something, some statement that they had made. And I saw some sort of paper with Mr. Cehajic in which it stated why -- what he was suspected of. Someone from the prosecution had written something down, something like that. I didn't sign anything. And I didn't discuss this matter for long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not answering the question, the question was, were any proceedings instituted against anyone else? You answered everything except the question. So what is your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is that I was told that some men had signed something and that proceedings were instituted against certain men.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a record made when you were questioned?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, what you last said about the meeting in the Chamber of Commerce in Banja Luka, you said that in the name of the SDS, Mr. Brdjanin proposed a candidate as president of the Chamber of Commerce and you said that his proposal was not accepted?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could we conclude that he couldn't order who should be appointed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that entire process in our opinion seemed to be arrogant, insolent. He appeared with that candidate. I can't remember who the candidate was any more but we didn't even vote about this candidate. We only voted on the proposal for Mr. Mersa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among the members of that assembly, of the Chamber of Commerce there were certain Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my conclusion is that Mr. Brdjanin's proposal didn't have enough authority to be accepted?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And it didn't go through the usual procedure that was adopted for a proposal, when a proposal was being put forward by a group in the assembly. That wasn't well defined at the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: One question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead. Re-examined by Mr. Waidyaratne:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, you were asked about your knowledge of the other detainees, as to whether there was proceedings instituted against them when they were in Omarska, and you said that some were -- that some people had charges against them or legal proceedings instituted against them. Do you know specific people whom you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I said that some people signed statements that they made and some people, such as Mr. Cehajic had a piece of paper in which it stated what they were suspected of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- [Previous translation continues] ... Were they taken to a court of law?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he survive the camp?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Murselovic, as you see, you managed to finish even before time. You will very soon be escorted by our usher out of this courtroom, and you will be given all the assistance you require to return to your country. However, before you leave this courtroom, it is my duty as the Presiding Judge, in my name and the name of the other two judges as well as on behalf of the Tribunal to thank you for having accepted to come back to The Hague to give evidence for the second time. I know it's not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. easy for anyone, and it's for this reason that I thank you once more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So now what's left, I suppose is the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, may I be permitted to tender into evidence the exhibit, the transcript from the Stakic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Marked as P1542 with the accompanying exhibits? Documents which were given numbers as P1452/S45, P1542/S46, P1542/S45-1, P1542/S46-1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that all right with you, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is, Your Honour. No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So these documents are being so admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for all your cooperation, both sides. Is there anything else before we wind up for the day?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to mention only one thing, according to order of witnesses, we scheduled one witness for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: 7.134 and one witness for fly day which is 7.54. I was informed that the witness 7.134 will take one hour, most probably less than one hour, and I was also informed that there won't be very lengthy cross-examination. So in fact, I -- I am seeking advice from you, whether it would be more convenient for you to hear two witnesses tomorrow or whether you would prefer to be present at the plenary and stick to the schedule as planned? It means one witness tomorrow and one witness on Friday. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, would it cause the Defence any disruption or any serious problems if we hear both witnesses tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it wouldn't cause any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if you are in a position to bring both witnesses tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, we will in position to bring the second one in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will hear their evidence tomorrow. I thank you, Madam Richterova. Tomorrow we will be sitting in the morning, I forgot whether it's this courtroom or some other courtroom. I think this courtroom is needed for the plenary. Courtroom I, we are meeting in tomorrow. I thank you once more. And good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 12.33 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 12th day of December, 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
